sermon:
## No Other Gospel
*The desertion that comes dressed as devotion*

**Text:** Galatians 1:1-24 · **Supporting:** Galatians 1:6-7; Galatians 1:11-12; Galatians 1:16; Galatians 2:21

Paul does not open this letter the way he opens the others. There is no thanksgiving. There is no warm word for the church before the work begins. He writes to people he loves, people he led to Christ, and the first thing out of his mouth after the greeting is astonishment. Something has gone wrong in Galatia, and it has not gone wrong by anyone walking away from God. It has gone wrong by people becoming more careful, more rigorous, more committed to getting it right. That is the part we never see coming. A church does not usually lose the gospel by abandoning it. It loses the gospel by improving it.

**The desertion no one called a desertion**

Hear what Paul actually says. "I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel — not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ." (Galatians 1:6-7) Read that slowly. He calls it deserting *him* — not deserting a doctrine, a person. And the Galatians would have been stunned to hear it, because in their own minds they were not deserting anyone. They were adding. They were taking the grace they had received and reinforcing it with the law, with circumcision, with the marks of belonging that had carried God's people for two thousand years. It felt like maturing. It felt like seriousness. It felt like the next step.

Paul will not let them keep the word *next*. He says there is no other gospel — that the thing they are reaching for is not a deeper version of what they had but a different thing entirely, wearing the old gospel's clothes. The distortion did not announce itself. Distortions never do. They come in offering more, and the more is the poison.

**Where the gospel came from, and where it did not**

Then Paul does something the rest of the chapter is built to do. He tells them where this message came from, because everything depends on it. "For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man's gospel. For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ." (Galatians 1:11-12) He spends the back half of the chapter walking through his own history — the persecutor, the zealot for the traditions of his fathers, the man who was advancing in Judaism beyond his peers — precisely to show that this message could not have been his own invention. He had every reason to invent the opposite. He was building a career on the opposite. "He who set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me." (Galatians 1:16) A gospel you receive cannot be edited by the one who received it. If men gave it to you, men can amend it. But if God gave it, your hands come off.

This is the foundation under everything Paul will say for six chapters. The reason the Galatians cannot add to grace is not that addition is impractical. It is that the gospel is not theirs to revise. It was handed down, not worked up. The moment a church believes the gospel is something it generates rather than something it received, the editing begins, and the editing is always in the direction of works, because works are the thing the human heart will always reach for when it is left alone with grace.

**Why we keep adding**

Now turn it around, because the Galatian instinct is not a first-century instinct. It is the instinct in the room right now. We do the same thing, and we do it for the same reason. Grace alone feels insufficient to us — not in our theology, where we will defend it, but in our bones, where we live. We believe Christ saved us, and then on Monday we set about earning the salvation we already have. We add the quiet ledger of our discipline. We add the comparison with the Christian across the aisle. We add the suspicion that God's affection rises and falls with our performance, so we perform. I have preached grace and then gone home and lived as though my standing with God were a balance I was responsible to keep from going negative. That is the Galatian heresy in a pulpit, and it does not feel like heresy. It feels like trying hard.

Paul's word for it is not gentle. He says that if anyone — even an angel from heaven — preaches a gospel that adds to the one they received, let him be accursed. And later in the letter he tells us why the stakes are that high: "if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose." (Galatians 2:21) That is the whole weight of it. To add a requirement to grace is not to honor the cross more. It is to say the cross was not enough. Every addition is a verdict on Calvary. The Christ who was crucified for you is either sufficient or he is decoration, and the law-plus-grace gospel quietly makes him decoration while singing his name. We were crucified with Christ — and a man who has died with Christ has no résumé left to submit. The only ground he stands on is the grace that called him.

The mercy here is severe and it is real. The same Paul who pronounces the curse is the man pronouncing it because he cannot bear to watch a church he loves trade a finished Savior for an unfinished self. The door he is guarding so fiercely is the door of pure grace, and he stands in it with his arms out because he knows what is on the other side.

Add to grace and lose it.

## Justified by Faith, Not Works of the Law
*The day Paul opposed Peter to his face*

**Text:** Galatians 2:1-21 · **Supporting:** Galatians 2:11-12; Galatians 2:16; Galatians 2:20; Galatians 2:21

There is a scene in this chapter that the church has never been quite comfortable with. Paul tells us that he opposed Peter — Peter, the rock, the one who walked with Jesus, the one to whom the keys were given — opposed him publicly, to his face, because Peter was wrong. Not wrong in his doctrine. Peter knew the doctrine. Wrong in his feet. Peter had been eating with Gentile believers, sitting at one table with them as equals in Christ, until certain men came from Jerusalem, and then Peter got up and moved. He withdrew. He drew back to the side of the line where the circumcised sat. And his quiet feet preached a sermon louder than any words: there are two tables here, and you Gentiles are at the lesser one until you earn your way to ours.

**The sermon Peter preached by moving his chair**

Watch exactly what Paul saw. "For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party." (Galatians 2:11-12) Fearing. That is the engine under the whole thing. Peter did not change his mind. Peter got scared. And fear is how the gospel gets bent in practice long before it gets bent in print. Nobody at that table stood up and announced a new doctrine of salvation by works. A man simply moved his chair, and in moving it he rebuilt the wall Christ had torn down. The gospel does not usually die in a council. It dies in a thousand small withdrawals, each one explainable, each one understandable, each one putting one more condition between a sinner and the table of grace.

Paul understood that conduct is doctrine when people are watching. He says Peter and the others "were not in step with the truth of the gospel." The truth had not changed in Peter's head. His walk had drifted out of step with it. And a church can confess sound theology with its mouth while its practices — who is welcome, who must change first, who sits at the lesser table — preach a different gospel entirely.

**The sentence the whole letter turns on**

So Paul tells him the truth, and in telling it he gives us the verse that the Reformation was eventually built on. "We know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified." (Galatians 2:16) Hear how he hammers it. Three times in one sentence: not by works of the law, but by faith; faith, not works of the law; by works of the law, no one. He is not being repetitive by accident. He is driving a stake through the center of the room. *Justified* is a courtroom word — it means the verdict of acquittal, the declaration that a guilty defendant is now counted righteous. And Paul says that verdict never comes through the defendant's performance. It comes through the defendant's faith in Another.

This is the hinge of everything. There are only two ways a human being has ever tried to stand before God: by what he has done, or by what Christ has done. There is no third. And Peter's drawn-back chair was an argument for the first way, made by a man who believed the second. That is why Paul could not let it pass. To rebuild the law as the ground of acceptance, Paul says, is to make Christ a servant of sin and to nullify the grace of God. "I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose." (Galatians 2:21) If you can be made right by your own performance, then Golgotha was a tragedy with no payload. The cross was either everything or it was nothing. There is no version where it was helpful.

**The chair I have moved**

And now the harder part, because it is easy to read this as a story about Peter. It is not. I have moved the chair. I have welcomed people in the language of grace and then, when the certain men came — when the people whose approval I wanted were watching — found reasons to draw back, to put a condition in front of someone, to make the table conditional on their looking more like me first. We do this. We do it about the wrong sins, the wrong politics, the wrong background, the wrong mess. We say grace and we live a quiet sorting. And the people on the lesser side of our drawn-back chairs hear the sermon our feet are preaching, even when our mouths are still saying the right words.

Paul's answer to Peter is the only answer that has ever set a sinner free, and it is the answer to us: "I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." (Galatians 2:20) A crucified man has no standing of his own to defend, no table of his own to guard, no ladder of acceptance to make others climb. He has died, and the life he has now is borrowed entirely from the One who loved him and gave himself for him. The man who truly believes that cannot move his chair, because he knows he sat down at that table on grace alone, and so did everyone else.

If law could save, Christ died needlessly.

## Abraham's Blessing and the Curse the Law Could Not Lift
*Counted righteous before the law was ever written*

**Text:** Galatians 3:1-29 · **Supporting:** Galatians 3:6; Galatians 3:10-11; Galatians 3:13; Galatians 3:29

Paul opens this chapter the way a grieving man speaks, not an angry one. "O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you?" He is watching people who began in the Spirit try to finish in the flesh, and he asks them one question that should have ended the argument: did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith? They knew the answer. They had been there. The Spirit had fallen on them when they believed, before they had performed anything, before they had taken on a single requirement. And now they wanted to add the requirements after the fact, as though the God who began the work by grace would somehow need their works to complete it.

**The man who was counted righteous before there was a law to keep**

To settle it, Paul reaches back past Moses, past Sinai, all the way to Abraham — and his timing is the whole argument. "Just as Abraham 'believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.'" (Galatians 3:6) Abraham was declared righteous in Genesis 15, by faith, four hundred and thirty years before the law was given at Sinai. Sit with the arithmetic, because Paul builds on it. The man God held up as the father of the faithful was justified before the law existed. So the law cannot be the ground of acceptance, because the first accepted man had no law to stand on. He had a promise, and he believed it, and God counted the believing as righteousness. The blessing was always a thing received by faith, never a wage earned by performance. Paul's conclusion is plain: "those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith." The true children of Abraham are not the ones with the right bloodline or the right marks. They are the ones who believe.

This matters because the Galatians thought they were climbing toward Abraham by taking up the law. Paul shows them they were climbing away from him. Abraham did not get in by law-keeping. Nobody does.

**The curse no amount of keeping could lift**

Then Paul names the thing the law actually does, and it is not what the Galatians hoped. "For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, 'Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.' Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for 'The righteous shall live by faith.'" (Galatians 3:10-11) Read the trap carefully. The law does not offer partial credit. It says *all things* — abide by all of it, do all of it, miss nothing. The law was never a ladder you could climb most of the way up and be graded on effort. It was a standard that cursed every single person who failed to keep the whole of it, which is every single person who has ever lived. To put yourself under the law as the ground of your standing is not to reach for blessing. It is to step under a curse you have no power to lift, because the requirement is perfection and you do not have it.

The law could diagnose the curse. The law could not lift it. And that is where the gospel comes into this chapter like a door opening in a wall there was no door in. "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, 'Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree.'" (Galatians 3:13) There it is. The curse you could not lift, he absorbed. He went up on the tree and took the very curse the law pronounced over your failure, became it, drank it down to the bottom, so that the blessing promised to Abraham could come to people who had earned only the curse. He did not lower the standard. He met it and then bore the penalty for everyone who never could. The law was satisfied — not by us climbing up to it, but by him going down under it.

**Stop tearing your own pardon in half**

And here is where it lands on us, because we are quieter Galatians than we admit. We believe Christ became a curse for us, and then we live as though the curse were still partly ours to manage. We treat the Christian life as a probation — saved by grace, retained by performance — and every failure sends us scrambling back under the law to repair a standing the cross already secured. I have done this from the pulpit and in my own chest at midnight, going back under the curse Christ already became for me, as though his cry of dereliction left a balance still owed. It is foolishness. It is the bewitching Paul names in verse one. To go back under the law after the cross is to tear up your own pardon and try to re-earn what was signed in blood.

Paul's final word in the chapter closes the door behind us so we cannot crawl back through it. "And if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise." (Galatians 3:29) Not heirs according to your law-keeping. Heirs according to promise — the same promise Abraham believed, the same righteousness counted to faith, the same blessing that comes to all who believe and to none who merely perform. We were crucified with Christ, and the curse died there with us. The inheritance is held out now by an empty hand, and it is received the only way it was ever received: by believing the God who gives it.

Faith receives what works could never earn.

## Sons and Heirs, No Longer Slaves
*The Spirit who cries Father in a freed man's chest*

**Text:** Galatians 4:1-31 · **Supporting:** Galatians 4:4-5; Galatians 4:6; Galatians 4:7; Galatians 4:9

Paul has been arguing about law and grace, faith and works, and now in chapter four he changes the picture. He stops talking like a lawyer and starts talking like a household. The question is no longer only *how is a man declared righteous* — it is *what is a man to God once he is*. And Paul's answer is the most intimate thing in the letter. Not a pardoned criminal kept at arm's length. Not a servant earning his keep in the great house. A son. Brought inside. Given the name. Made an heir. The whole chapter turns on the distance between a slave and a son, and on the strange fact that the freed man keeps trying to walk back into the chains.

**The fullness of time, and the Son sent to make sons**

First Paul shows us where sonship came from, and he roots it in a precise moment in history, not a timeless idea. "But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons." (Galatians 4:4-5) Hear the shape of it. The Son was sent — sent into a real woman, into a real history, into a real subjection under the very law that held us. He was born under the law so that he could redeem those under the law. The free One stepped into the slavery to buy out the slaves. And the goal Paul names is not merely that we would be acquitted, but that we would be adopted — that the redemption would not stop at a clean record but go all the way to a family name. God did not send his Son so that we could be his employees. He sent his Son so that we could be his children.

Adoption is a verdict and a relationship at once. The law could make demands. The law could never make sons. Only the sending of the Son into the curse could turn slaves into heirs, and that is exactly what God set out to do from the fullness of time.

**The Spirit who proves it from the inside**

Then Paul moves the proof from the courtroom into the chest, because a man can be told he is a son and still feel like a slave. So God gives the assurance from the inside. "And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, 'Abba! Father!'" (Galatians 4:6) Notice the order — *because you are sons*, God sent the Spirit. The Spirit does not make us sons by our feeling him. The Spirit is given because we already are sons, and his work is to make the relationship real in our experience, to put on our lips the one word a slave would never dare say to his master: Father. Abba is the word of a child who is certain of his welcome, certain of his place, certain he will not be put out. The Spirit of the Son speaks the Son's own word in us, so that the freed man's heart catches up to the freed man's status.

And Paul draws the conclusion with the simplest sentence in the chapter. "So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God." (Galatians 4:7) No longer. The status changed and it does not flicker. A son does not earn his place in the family — he was given it. A son does not work to become an heir — the inheritance comes to him by birth, by the father's choice, not by his labor. Everything a slave strives for, a son already possesses. That is the gospel: not that God hired you on probation, but that he made you his own and wrote you into the will.

**Why do we keep walking back into the chains?**

So Paul cannot understand what the Galatians are doing, and neither should we, because we are doing it too. "But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?" (Galatians 4:9) Read that and feel the grief in it. They were sons, and they were trying to re-enlist as slaves. They had the Father's name on their lips and were reaching back for the master's yoke. And we do this with our own version of the elementary principles — our rules, our religious performance, our spiritual scorekeeping — the weak and worthless things we keep crawling back under because slavery, for all its misery, at least lets us feel we are paying our own way. There is a strange comfort in earning. It keeps the relationship on our terms. Sonship is harder to believe precisely because it is free, and the heart that has spent its life paying does not trust a gift it did not buy.

I have lived as a slave in my Father's house, working anxiously for an inheritance already written in my name, treating the family table like a wage I had to keep deserving. It is the most ungrateful thing a son can do, and it is the most natural. We were crucified with Christ — the slave we used to be died on that tree — and the Spirit of the Son was sent into our hearts to say the word the slave could never say. The cure for our anxious laboring is not more laboring. It is to hear the Spirit cry *Abba* from inside our own chest and to believe, against every instinct that wants to earn, that the Father meant it when he made us sons.

A son does not earn his inheritance.

## Free, and Walking by the Spirit
*The freedom that is not a license but a road*

**Text:** Galatians 5:1-26 · **Supporting:** Galatians 5:1; Galatians 5:6; Galatians 5:13; Galatians 5:22-23

Every argument Paul has made comes to a single command at the start of chapter five, and it stands almost alone on the page. "For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery." (Galatians 5:1) For freedom — that is the purpose, not a side effect. Christ did not redeem us so we could trade one set of chains for a more religious set. He set us free for freedom itself, and then Paul says the surprising thing: *stand firm*. Freedom, it turns out, is not a thing you drift into. It is a thing you have to hold your ground to keep, because there are forces on both sides trying to take it back — the legalist pulling you toward the yoke of law, and the flesh pulling you toward the yoke of appetite. The chapter is Paul standing the freed church between those two thieves and telling it to stand firm.

**The freedom legalism wants to take**

The first thief is the one Paul has been fighting all along. The Galatians were being told that faith in Christ was a fine beginning but that real standing with God required the law's marks — circumcision, the whole code. And Paul says the moment you make any of that the ground of your acceptance, the freedom is gone. "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love." (Galatians 5:6) There is the standard, and notice it is not nothing — it is not lawlessness. It is *faith working through love*. Not the law as a ladder, and not freedom as an excuse, but faith that is alive, faith that moves, faith that spends itself in love. The legalist wants to add requirements to faith. Paul says faith already works — it works through love — and the moment you bolt the law back on as the ground of standing, you have severed yourself from the grace that was carrying you. Stand firm. Do not put the yoke back on.

**The freedom the flesh wants to abuse**

But Paul knows the other thief is in the room too, and this is where so much preaching on freedom goes wrong — it warns about the law and forgets the flesh. So Paul names the second danger in the same breath. "For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another." (Galatians 5:13) There is the hinge of the whole chapter. The flesh hears the word *free* and reads it as *do what you want*. The flesh wants to take the open door Christ purchased and use it as cover for the same old appetites — now baptized, now permitted, now spiritual. And Paul says no. The freedom Christ bought is not a license for the self. It is room — room to walk a road you could not walk before. The road is the Spirit. "Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh." Freedom is not the absence of a master. It is the exchange of a cruel master for a true one. The flesh promises liberty and delivers slavery; the Spirit looks like surrender and delivers the only freedom there is.

Paul lays the two roads side by side — the works of the flesh, ugly and obvious, and the fruit of the Spirit, which grows where the Spirit walks. "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law." (Galatians 5:22-23) Notice it is fruit, not works — not a performance the flesh strains to produce, but the natural yield of a life rooted in the Spirit. You do not manufacture patience by clenching your jaw. It grows on the branch that abides. And the first of the fruit is love, which is exactly what Paul said freedom was for: "through love serve one another." The whole law, he says, is fulfilled in one word — you shall love your neighbor as yourself. The freed man does not use his freedom to grab. He uses it to serve.

**The freedom we keep handing back**

And here is where it finds us, because we are skilled at losing this freedom in both directions. Some of us hand it back to the legalist — we cannot rest in grace, so we re-yoke ourselves with rules and scorekeeping and the anxious labor of staying acceptable. And some of us hand it to the flesh — we hear *free in Christ* and quietly use it to excuse the thing we always wanted to do, calling our appetite liberty. I have done both, sometimes in the same week — re-shackled myself with religious performance on Tuesday and let my freedom cover my flesh on Friday. Both are the loss of the freedom Christ died to give. Both are a freed man walking back toward a yoke.

The answer to both is not a third yoke. It is the Spirit. "Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires." We were crucified with Christ — and the flesh that the legalist tries to discipline and the flesh that the libertine tries to indulge was nailed there with him. The freedom Christ bought is the room to walk by the Spirit down a road the flesh could never travel, bearing fruit the law could only ever demand and never grow. Stand firm in it. Do not give it back to either thief.

Freedom serves through love, not self.

## Bearing Burdens, Boasting Only in the Cross
*The one ground of boasting a freed man has left*

**Text:** Galatians 6:1-18 · **Supporting:** Galatians 6:2; Galatians 6:7-8; Galatians 6:9; Galatians 6:14

A letter that has spent six chapters tearing down every false ground of standing has to end somewhere, and Paul ends it on the ground that is left. Not the law. Not circumcision. Not the marks of belonging the false teachers were so proud of. The cross — and nothing else. But before he gets there he shows what a Spirit-walking life actually looks like on the ground, on a Tuesday, among people, because the freedom he has been defending was never meant to stay an idea. A church that has truly received grace does something with its hands. It bends down under the weight of the person next to it.

**The body that carries its own**

Paul has just laid out the fruit of the Spirit, and now he shows the fruit at work. When someone is caught in a sin, the spiritual ones restore him gently, watching themselves lest they fall too. And then the command that names the whole texture of a grace-shaped church: "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ." (Galatians 6:2) Hear what that does. The law the Galatians wanted to take up was a law you carried alone — every man under the weight of his own perfect performance, every man cursed by his own failure. The law of Christ is the opposite. It is a weight you carry *together*. The legalist's religion isolates; each soul stands alone before the standard. The Spirit's community gets underneath each other. The freedom Christ bought does not produce a crowd of self-made individuals proud of their own keeping. It produces a body that stoops to carry the one who is failing. That is how the law of Christ — love your neighbor — actually gets fulfilled. Not by climbing higher. By bending lower.

**The harvest no one cheats**

Then Paul names a law that runs underneath all of this, sober and unflinching. "Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that he will also reap. For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life." (Galatians 6:7-8) This is not legalism creeping back in. This is the seriousness of a real life lived in the Spirit. The freedom Christ gave is not a freedom from consequence — it is the freedom to sow to the Spirit, and what you sow you will reap. A life spent feeding the flesh harvests the rot of the flesh. A life spent walking by the Spirit harvests what the Spirit gives. And because the harvest is slow and the sowing is daily and unglamorous, Paul adds the word every tired believer needs: "And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up." (Galatians 6:9) The bearing of burdens is wearying. The doing of good in a body of broken people is wearying. Paul does not pretend otherwise. He simply tells us the harvest is coming, in its season, for the ones who do not quit.

**The only boast a crucified man has left**

And then Paul ends the letter where the whole letter was always going. The false teachers, he says, wanted to make a good showing in the flesh — they wanted to boast in the marks they put on the Galatians' bodies, to count converts to the law as trophies. Paul will have none of it. "But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world." (Galatians 6:14) There is the bottom of everything. Strip away the law, strip away the performance, strip away every mark a man could point to and say *this is why I stand* — and what is left for a Christian to boast in is one thing: a Roman instrument of execution on which the Son of God died for him. Paul has no other ground. The cross has cut him off from the world's whole economy of boasting; the world is dead to him and he to it. The man who boasts in the cross cannot boast in himself, because the cross is precisely the announcement that he had nothing to bring.

And now it turns onto us, because we are all looking for something to boast in, even at church — especially at church. We point quietly to our doctrine, our discipline, our giving, our rightness, our record. We do the Galatian thing in subtler clothes: we find a mark we can show and we lean our standing on it. I have boasted in my ministry, my orthodoxy, my labor, in the very work of preaching grace — turning even grace into a trophy. And every one of those boasts is a quiet desertion of the cross, because every one of them says there is some ground of mine to stand on besides Christ crucified. There is not. We were crucified with Christ. The man who has died on that cross has no résumé left to present and no trophy left to raise. He has only the cross, and the cross is enough, because justification was never by anything we carried up to God — it was by faith in the One who carried the curse down for us.

So the letter ends as it began: no other gospel, no other ground, no other boast. The world is dead to the man who has seen the cross, and he is dead to it, and what rises in that death is a son who carries his brother's burden and boasts in nothing but the blood.

Boast in the cross or boast in nothing.
